Root Word
• A root word is a word in its most basic word form.
• It is a word that does not have a prefix or a suffix.
• It is a complete word that cannot be broken down further.

Example:
The root word “mask” is a noun.
Place the word “un” in front of “mask,” and it
becomes “unmask,” which is a verb.
Mask (noun) It is a thing.
Unmask (verb) It is an action

“a-”
• Prefix a-
• We can use the prefix a- to make some words, usually adjectives, negative.
• typical – atypical; theist – atheist; political – apolitical; social – asocial
Sentence examples:
Pronoun V ADJ
He does not like to party with his classmates because he is asocial.
(article) (noun)
Since he is an atheist, he does not go to church on Sundays.
S V ADJ
This bird is atypical because it does not build a nest like other birds.
Cuckoo! Cuckoo!

“ab-”
• Prefix ab–
• Very few words take the negative prefix ab-.
• duct – abduct; use – abuse
Sentence examples:
He was abducted by aliens.
In most cases, those who have authority abuse their power.

“anti-”
• The prefix anti- originates from Greek and it
means ‘opposite’ or ‘against’.
• In most cases, it requires a hyphen. This is a
hyphen: “–”
• clockwise – anti-clockwise; social – anti-social;
aging – anti-aging;

“de-”
• The Prefix de-
• It is almost always used before a verb or a word formed from a
verb.
• It means to reverse the verb's action.
• hydrate – dehydrate; regulate – deregulate; toxify – detoxify
Sentence examples:
The nurses made sure I did not dehydrate.
You can detoxify your body by reducing your coffee intake.

“dis-”
• Prefix dis-
• The negative prefix dis- means not, so it gives the opposite meaning when added to the
word.
• like – dislike; comfort – discomfort; similar – dissimilar.
Sentence examples:
I dislike people who are late for appointments.
She felt a slight discomfort when the dentist was removing her braces.
They have such dissimilar tastes in music that they can’t agree on what to listen to on the car radio.

“in-”
• Prefix in-
• This negative prefix is normally used with words starting with ac or c:
• competent – incompetent; visible – invisible; efficient – inefficient; sane – insane
Sentence examples:
I was incompetent at playing the piano.
Harry Potter had a cloak that could turn him invisible.
He must be insane if he thinks pigs can fly and speak Latin.

“im-”
• Prefix im-
• This prefix normally goes with adjectives that begin with the letter p:
• personal – impersonal; perfect – imperfect; possible – impossible
Sentence examples:
Her children found her to be distant and impersonal.
Imperfect goods are sold cheaply.
This puzzle is impossible to solve.

“il”
• Prefix il-
• This prefix is used with words that start with the letter “L.”
• logical – illogical; legible – illegible; literate – illiterate.
Sentence examples:
His way of thinking is completely illogical.
Most doctors have illegible handwriting.
Most coal miners in poor countries are illiterate because
they started working from a young age and never received a
proper education.

“ir-”
• Prefix ir-
• Use it with the words starting with the
letter r:
• replaceable – irreplaceable; rational–
irrational; regular – irregular.
Sentence examples:
Please be careful, for that item is irreplaceable.
He has an irrational fear of balloons.
I went to see the doctor because of irregular
breathing.

“mal-”
• The prefix mal-
• It is usually added to change the meaning to negative and refers
to bad, unpleasant, or unsuccessful things.
• nutrition – malnutrition; nourish – malnourish; practice –
malpractice
Sentence examples:
Pets that are neglected and are not fed by their owners often suffer from
malnutrition.
She was malnourished after spending 40 days in the desert.
His doctor was found guilty of malpractice.

“mis-”
• Prefix mis-
• Prefix mis- means false or wrong.
• lead – mislead; fortune – misfortune, spell – misspell
Sentence examples:
The company mislead us with false advertising.
The family suffered great misfortune.
When I was a child, I would often misspell words.

“non-”
• The prefix non-
• It is used with adjectives and nouns, but never with verbs.
• It is often written with hyphen:
• existent – non-existent; specific – non-specific; refundable – non-refundable
Sentence examples:
Do not worry about problems that are non-existent.
Non-specific answers could lead to a low score on your quiz.
These items are non-refundable.

“un-”
• Prefix un-
• The prefix un- is the most commonly used negative prefix.
• friendly – unfriendly: real – unreal; fit – unfit;
Sentence examples:
My neighbors acts unfriendly towards me.
The whole situation seemed unreal to me.
He is unfit for the job.

Lesson 1
Part 2
Prefixes that relate to positions and levels
a- pre- post- im- ininter- trans- up- outover- under- extra-

a- (in, on, at,)
• in: root word: bed;
She is resting abed after her long trip.
(resting in bed)
• on: root word: board;
He was already aboard the plane by the time I arrived.
(He was on the plane)
• at: root word: shore;
We arrived ashore this morning
(Arrived at the shore)
Sea turtles come ashore to lay their eggs. (at/on the shore)

pre- (before)
Examples:
Preorder (Ordering an item before it is available)
Preview (Viewing something before it is displayed or becomes available to the public)
Predate (Existing or occuring at a date that is before (something)
Sentence Examples:
I preordered this video game before it was released.
I saw a sneak preview of the new Daredevil series that is coming to Disney+.
The Stone Age predates the Bronze Age.

post- (after/later)
Examples:
• Post-production (working on a movie after filming is completed/editing process)
• Postpone (arrange for something to take place later than what was first scheduled)
• Postgraduate (a student who studies after getting their Bachelor’s degree)
Extra Info: Undergraduates are students who are studying for their Bacherlor’s degree.
Postgraduate can also be used as an adjective. (posgraduate degree, postgraduate year, postgraduate students, etc)
Sentence Examples:
The movie is now in post-production.
Can we postpone the due date?
Postgraduate students often choose study abroad.

im- (into, in)
Examples:
• Implant (to insert tissue or artificial object into someone’s body)
• Import (bring goods into a country/transfer into a file or document)
• Imprint (Mark a surface by pressing something into it)
Sentence Examples:
I got dental implants after breaking my two front teeth.
I imported the photos from my camera into my computer.
His footprints were imprinted in the mud.

in- (into/in)
Examples:
• Inside (The inner part of something)
• Input (what is put in, or taken in by a process or system)
(the action of putting or feeding something in)
• Internal (inner parts or features)
Sentences examples:
He went inside the building.
Edit the input text and re-run the software.
Your liver is an internal organ.
An internal hard drive is a computer’s primary storage device.

inter-(between, from one to another)
Examples:
• Internet (Networks that exist between each other)
• International (Between nations)
Sentence Examples:
Without the internet, I cannot download the new DLC for Witcher 3.
Most 5 star hotels have an international buffet.

trans- (across, into another thing)
Examples:
• Transform (change into another thing)
• Transplant (move or transfer something across to another place or situation)
• Transfer (move from one place to another)
Sentence examples:
During a full moon he transforms into a werewolf.
The doctor is performing a kidney transplant.
I need to transfer all my data into an external hard drive.

up- (higher, upwards)
Examples:
• Uphold (to keep up or keep from sinking; support)
(to lift upward; raise)
• Uphill (direction up a hill or slope)
Sentence Examples:
It is a judge’s duty to uphold the law.
The pillar upheld the building’s heavy roof.
This is an uphill road.

Scientist are always trying to find extraterrestrial life outside our solar system.

• To the best of your abilities, match the following definitons to the correct word.
• You may not use a dictionary or any electronic devices to help you.
entitle: defintion # _____ embody: defintion # _____
inflame: defintion # _____ impregnate: definition # ____
Definitions:
1. provoke or intensify (strong feelings, especially anger) in someone.
2. be an expression of or give a tangible or visible form to (an idea, quality, or feeling).
3. make (a woman or female animal) pregnant.
4. give (someone) a legal right or a just claim to receive or do something.

Prefixes Are Not Always Direct
• Sometimes prefixes can change the entire meaning of a word making it difficult to figure out the meaning. Just understanding the meaning behind prefixes is
not enough.
Example of a meaning being changed to a direct opposite meaning.
Popular: liked or admired by other people
Unpopular: not liked or admired by other people
Example of a word’s meaning being completely changed.
Bringing: take or go with (someone or something) to a place.
Upbringing: the treatment and instruction received by a child from its parents throughout its childhood.
As you can see, by adding the prefix “up-” the meaning does not simply become “to take or go with something in an upward direction.”
Therefore, if you are unsure with certain words that have prefixes, then you should use a dictionary to guide you.

text:
Extra Information
There are root words that can contain both prefixes & suffixes
Example:
Root Word: do
Prefix: un- Suffix: -ble
un- = (opposite) -able = (able to)
do = Perform an action
undo = Cancel or reverse the previous action
doable = An action that can be completed
undoable = An action that cannot be completed
undoable
